paras: The flight of Booker T. Washington Jr. from Alabama was his reported departure from the state in late 1918, after Black newspapers said he had denounced a mob that lynched a Black man at Sheffield, Alabama, named some of its members, and was then threatened with mob vengeance. No one was killed in the episode; Washington Jr., son of the founder of Tuskegee Institute, was said to have fled with his family to Ohio and then St. Louis. The story ran in at least ten Black weeklies in January 1919, though a Chattanooga minister denied that anyone had run him out of the state.

According to the syndicated account, Washington Jr. was claim adjuster for Black employees at the Muscle Shoals war plant, which employed nine thousand men. A St. Louis Argus item of March 1919 identified the lynching he had spoken against as that of "Will Bryd and Wm Whiteide" [Byrd and Whiteside].

In the fullest version, datelined Tuskegee, December 23, in the Colorado Statesman and St. Louis, January 14, in the Phoenix Tribune, Washington Jr. named some of the Sheffield mob and demanded that they be brought to justice. He then fled for his life with his wife and children, traveling with the aid of white friends into Ohio while "small bands were holding up vehicles and searching the trains in every direction." A Cleveland dispatch of January 1, printed by the Baltimore Afro-American as unconfirmed rumor, placed him in Ohio as "a refugee from mob violence."

After several days he reportedly returned to Tuskegee, where friendly whites warned him of plots to take vengeance on him for his stand against "the Sheffield outrage" and said they could not protect him. He left again under cover of darkness for St. Louis.

A Chicago dispatch of April 14 reported him in that city, through with the South for good, and by late May he was said to be living in New York and working for the War Camp Community Service. The coverage reports no charges against anyone for threatening him; the Tuscumbia trials it mentions, which ended in two acquittals, concerned the Sheffield lynching itself.

The January story spread under headlines such as "BOOKER WASHINGTON FLEES, HUNTED BY ALABAMA MOR [MOB]" in the Dayton Forum, which credited the Pampa Bulletin, and "Booker Washington, Jr., Chased By Mob" in the Kansas City Sun and the Metropolis Weekly Gazette. Other copies ran between January 11 and 25 in papers including the Dallas Express, the Cleveland Gazette, the Black Dispatch and the Philadelphia Tribune.

The Dayton Forum wrote that "the criminal-minded minority in Alabama again blots the fair name of the state," and the Cleveland Gazette headed its copy "His Father's 'Best Friends of the Negro' Would Lynch-Murder the Son." In the New York Age, letters from Emmett J. Scott and an attorney objected to a New York Independent article about young Washington at Muscle Shoals, though the printed text is too damaged to give their full argument.

Through the spring the episode served as a reference point: the Omaha Monitor wrote that he was driven out "because he was not an apologist," and a speaker quoted by the Kansas City Advocate said that had he not escaped "he would now be with his father in the other world."

Rev. J. C. Robinson of Chattanooga, speaking at Columbia, South Carolina, said he had been at Sheffield, had condemned the lynching unmolested, and that "nobody ran Booker T. Washington Jr. away from Alabama." Accounts also differed on the cause: the January story cited his naming of mob members, while C. B. Hosmer, a Tuskegee field secretary, attributed it to his having members of a mob indicted. The Baltimore Afro-American said in April that he had telegraphed news of a lynching to the War Department, that "Crackers" then formed a mob and demanded his life, and that army officers drove him at night to relatives in Ohio.

bases: Black papers reported that Washington Jr. was threatened by a mob and forced to flee Alabama with his family (A8, A7, A22), though one witness denied it (A14).
No one was killed: Washington Jr. was threatened and escaped (A8, A22); the lynching the papers mention is the separate Sheffield case (A18).
Several independent reports say he was driven out (A2, A8, A19, A22), but Rev. J. C. Robinson denied anyone ran him away (A14), and the reports disagree on the cause.

framing.detail: Dayton Forum: 'In the Land of Democracy!' and 'the criminal-minded minority in Alabama again blots the fair name of the state'.
Cleveland Gazette: 'His Father's "Best Friends of the Negro" Would Lynch-Murder the Son', asking whether the South is in the 'world'.
Kansas City Sun: the story 'should be cabled to President Wilson, Principal Moton and the World's Peace Conference'.
Omaha Monitor editorial contrasts Washington Jr., driven out for not being an apologist, with Moton.
Baltimore Afro-American editorial lists his expulsion among 'bits of every day news from Southern states'.
Baltimore Afro-American printed both the rumor (as unconfirmed) and Rev. Robinson's denial under 'What Did Booker T. Do'.
